Deliverable 03 · one-page note

Data & methodology

How a snapshot of published facility information became a task-specific comparison tool—and where interpretation must stop.

QuestionCollectionDefinitionsScoringLimitations

Question & users

What space best fits the work?

The primary users are Harvard students choosing among study settings. A second audience is Harvard Library staff deciding which metadata and service improvements would make spaces easier to use. The unit of analysis is one named study space or study area, not a building and not an individual seat.

Collection

30 spaces, six libraries, one documented snapshot

Records were transcribed on 21 September 2026 from Harvard Library’s official Find a Space directory and checked against official pages for Cabot, Lamont, Widener, Harvard-Yenching, Loeb Music, and Fine Arts.

The sample is purposive rather than random: it includes prominent general-use libraries and smaller specialty libraries, with open areas, carrels, group rooms, media rooms, and presentation spaces. No personal or sensitive data was collected.

Important coding rule: a 1 means the feature was explicitly listed or stated on an official source page. A 0 means “not listed in the reviewed source,” not “the feature definitely does not exist.”

Units & definitions

Binary published-feature indicators

FieldUnitDefinition
Space / library / level / typeTextLabels used in the official directory, normalized only for consistency.
Quiet designated0 or 1Official card or library description explicitly indicates quiet or silent study.
Accessibility listed0 or 1Space card lists wheelchair or mobility-device accessibility.
Reservable listed0 or 1Official source states that the space can be booked or reserved.
Amenity fields0 or 1Charging, food/café, private desks, soft seating, display, whiteboard, or tech loan is listed.
24-hour building0 or 1The library page describes the building as a 24-hour library. This does not guarantee every room is available at every hour.
Fit score0–100 pointsWeighted sum of published features for one selected goal.

Scoring

Ratings are task-specific, not popularity ratings

Fit score = sum of the selected goal’s weights when a record has the corresponding published feature.

Deep focus prioritizes quiet designation (28 points) and private desks (24), followed by charging, accessibility, reservability, carrel/independent-room type, soft seating, and a 24-hour building. Group work prioritizes a group/meeting space type, whiteboards, reservability, displays, accessibility, charging, tech loan, and food/café. Make & present emphasizes media/meeting space, display, tech, whiteboards, charging, accessibility, reservability, and food/café. Comfort break emphasizes soft seating, food/café, charging, accessibility, private desks, open-space type, and a 24-hour building.

The weights are an explicit analytic choice. They make comparison reproducible but do not represent Harvard policy or surveyed student preferences.

Missing data, bias & uncertainty

What could change the result

  • Coverage: 30 spaces are not the full Harvard Library system; school-specific and non-library study areas are underrepresented.
  • Documentation bias: libraries that publish richer cards will score better even when another space has the same unlisted amenity.
  • No demand data: the dataset lacks occupancy, wait times, seat counts, or reservation usage, so it cannot identify crowding.
  • No satisfaction data: the fit score is not a student rating. No survey responses were collected.
  • Time sensitivity: hours, access rules, room equipment, and construction conditions can change; users should check current library pages before visiting.
  • Value judgment: weights encode one interpretation of each goal. Different users may value light, temperature, proximity, or social atmosphere—variables not present here.

The dashboard therefore supports comparison, metadata auditing, and hypothesis generation. It cannot prove that one space is objectively best or that an investment will improve student outcomes.
